Testimony in Support of LD 590 Date: 1/21/26
Good morning Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury and members of the Joint Standing
Committee on State and Local Government. My name is Beth Allen and I am here today
representing the Coalition on Racial Equity (CORE) to testify in strong support for LD 590, "An Act Regarding the Inclusion of Racial and Other Demographic Data from State Agencies in the
Legislative Process."
CORE actively pursues racial equity and justice by dismantling structural inequities and
disparities. We aspire to a world where influential decision-makers actively collaborate with
affected people and communities, fostering a collective effort to dismantle oppressive laws, policies, and practices for a more equitable and just society.
LD 590 builds on the work of this committee that began in the 130th Legislaturel completed in
the 131st Legislaturez to establish standards across state governments for how data is
collected, stored, and accessed by the public, and to provide policymakers with a better understanding of our population. Valid and informative data is essential to understand the scope of social, economic and health inequities in our state. Careful examination of that data will help identify the factors contributing to them, and ongoing monitoring of the data is critical to ensure progress towards comprehensive, long-term reductions in disparities.
LD 590 will designate a position in the Office of Policy and Legal Analysis to complete this examination using existing resources. This data will help state legislators and stakeholders gain important insights into the impact of potential legislation on individuals across Maine, especially on communities that have been historically disadvantaged. This information would be based on demographic data including, but not limited to, gender, location, race, ethnicity, birth sex, citizenship, socioeconomic status, education, sexual orientation, veteran status, disability status and age? The Office of Policy and Legal Analysis has experience and expertise conducting bill analysis in an efficient and timely manner, and is the logical department to oversee this work.
Maine and the United States have an unfortunate, long history of enacting policies that disadvantage people of color that have created generations of economic and social disparities.` To avoid making these worse, and to address existing inequalities, lawmakers need to be

Karen Blakelock, Policy Advisor The Nature Conservancy in Maine Karen.blakelock@tnc.org
Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government
RE: LD 590 - An Act Regarding the Inclusion of Racial and Other Demographic Data from State Agencies in the Legislative Process
Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government, my name is Karen Blakelock, and I work for The Nature Conservancy in Maine. I appreciate this opportunity testify in support of LD 590 - An Act Regarding the Inclusion of Racial and Other Demographic Data from State Agencies in the Legislative Process.
The Nature Conservancy (TNC) is a nonprofit conservation organization dedicated to conserving the lands and waters on which all life depends. Guided by science, we create innovative, on-the-ground solutions to our world's toughest challenges so that nature and people can thrive together. We use a collaborative approach that engages local communities, governments, the private sector, and other partners. The Nature Conservancy has been leading conservation in Maine for more than 60 years and is the 12th largest landowner in the state, owning and managing roughly 300,000 acres. We also work across Maine to restore rivers and streams, partner with fishermen in the Gulf of Maine to rebuild groundfish populations and develop innovative solutions to address our changing climate.
TNC is especially grateful for the leadership of Senator Talbot Ross on this bill, as a science-based organization, The Nature Conservancy is of the opinion that more data will help us make more informed decisions.
Our organization has come to understand that centering equity in our work is critical to achieving TNC's vision of a world where "the diversity of life thrives". Conservation does not happen in a vacuum. The work of conserving natural places inevitably intersects with and affects human communities in ways that create both benefits and burdens. As conservationists and as people, it is our responsibility to understand the full range of these impacts--especially the burdens they impose on communities that have historically experienced oppression and marginalization and still do today.
TNC supports this bill, and we see it as a step towards more future action on environmental justice in Maine. We are committed to pursuing measures to ensure the equitable distribution of environmental benefits and burdens, addressing cumulative impacts to environmental justice populations, and exploring how Maine agencies might develop specific community engagement plans in all decision making. Incorporating demographic data in instances where the state already has access to it into legislative decision making will help ensure that environmental justice and equity work takes place across all branches of government.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment in support of LD 590. I am happy to answer questions now or in the future.

Testimony in Support of LD 590, "An Act Regarding the Inclusion of Racial and Other Demographic Data from State Agencies in the Legislative Process" Karin Leuthy, Community Engagement Manager January 21, 2026

Good morning, Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
State and Local Government. My name is Karin Leuthy, and I'm the Community Engagement Manager at the
Maine Center for Economic Policy. I'm here to testify in support of LD 590, "An Act Regarding the Inclusion of Racial and Other Demographic Data from State Agencies in the Legislative Process," because MECEP knows good data is the foundation of good policy making.
We all know how powerful legislation can be in impacting Mainers' lives. LD 590 would give legislators,
advocates and members of the public access to more information on exactly which people would be most
affected by bills under consideration, especially vulnerable or disadvantaged groups.
At MECEP, we believe that all Mainers deserve a fair chance at economic success. But right now, some Mainers face extra barriers to achieving prosperity. Some of those obstacles were created by prior policy decisions, and
can only be undone through conscious effort in the legislature.
LD 590 allows the Office of Policy and Legal Analysis to look at a wide range of demographic data, and while
Mainers of Color face some of the biggest and longest-standing hurdles in our economy, we know that other groups face their own burdens which can be worsened or alleviated through policy choices. Women, older
Mainers, Mainers living in rural areas, and Mainers with disabilities all deserve attention in the policymaking
process.
Finally, I want to note that LD 590 fills a need that can't be met elsewhere. While groups like MECEP can provide legislators with some data on the impacts of bills on particular groups, we're limited by what's available in public datasets. These don't always have the level of detail we'd like, and when they are based on
national surveys, they sometimes don't produce reliable estimates at the state level for small demographic groups. LD 590 will allow OPLA to request administrative data from state agencies which can give us a more detailed and precise picture than survey data.
LD 590 will allow you to make more informed decisions with and build an economy that works for all Mainers. I urge you to vote "ought to pass."
Thank you for your time. I'll be happy to answer any questions.

Testimony in support of LD 590, An Act Regarding the Inclusion of
Racial and Other Demographic Data from State Agencies in the

January 21, 2026
Good morning Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and members of the Joint Standing
Committee on State and Local Government. My name is Kathy Kilrain del Rio. I use she/her pronouns and I'm the Advocacy & Programs Director at Maine Equal Justice, a nonprofit civil legal
aid and economic justice organization working to increase economic security, opportunity, and
equity for people in Maine. I am testifying today in support of the LD 590 and the sponsor's
proposed amendment.

When legislators are making decisions about proposed changes to Maine law, it is essential they have data to determine how the policies they are considering will impact different populations in
Maine. We know policies can have different impacts for different populations - whether that is
intentional or not. Knowing about those impacts prior to deciding on your support for legislation can help legislators make better informed decisions about policies.
Data tells us that there are significant socio-economic disparities based on race, ethnicity, tribal
status, and other demographics in Maine. We see this when we look at the data in systems like
education, health care, housing, employment, income, wealth, criminal justice, and more. Since
these systems all intersect and contribute to overall wealth, it's not surprising that we see some of
the starkest of these disparities in poverty rates. For us at Maine Equal Justice, this is most notable when looking at poverty data.

Census data illustrates disparities in poverty rates. (https://www.mecep.org/blog/census-data-shows-most-mainers-ahead-compared-to-pre-pandemic-b
ut-poorest-still-struggling/) 10.4% of Mainers who identify as White, Non Hispanic are living in poverty. Mainers who identify as Hispanic, American Indian, or of two or more races all experience higher rates of poverty with the highest rate - 26% - experienced by Black Mainers. The disparities we see in different areas are the result of a complex set of factors, including unfair laws and policies.

As lawmakers, you have a significant role in not only working to undo the effects of structural racism in our laws, but to also prevent further hann as you consider new laws. Furthermore, you have the opportunity to be proactive with policies that intentionally work to reduce disparities. The stark racial disparities in poverty in our state Won't begin to change until we craft laws that
explicitly target those disparities. For example, in the 130th legislative session, when the HHS
Committee was considering legislation to expand eligibility to the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) to 300%, data provided during the process showed that this would benefit a majority of Maine children - and it would also reduce disparities in health care coverage for Black,
Indigenous, and children of color. At the time, it was estimated that 43.7% of BIPOC children in th6
income range impacted by the bill were uninsured while 23.5% of white children in that income
range lacked health insurance. (https://legislature.maine.gov/testimony/resources/HHS20210224Pilotl32911396791438388.pdf)
By ultimately passing this law, legislators helped children of all races while also proactively addressing historical inequities for BIPOC children.
Lawmakers need the best information available to inform your decisions around questions of
positive or negative impact for different demographics. LD 5 90 would provide you with additional
information from a nonpartisan source when you are considering legislation.
Thank you for your consideration. We urge you to vote Ought to Pass on LD 590. I 'm happy to
answer any questions you may have.

Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government, my name is Lisa Margulies, I serve as Vice President of Public Affairs, Maine, for Planned Parenthood of Northern New England, and I am pleased to submit testimony in support of LD 590.
PPNNE provides comprehensive reproductive and sexual health care to approximately 10,000 patients per year in Maine at four health centers located in Biddeford, Portland, Sanford, and Topsham, in addition to online via telehealth. People turn to us for affordable, highest quality care including wellness exams, birth control, disease testing and treatment, cancer screenings, immunizations, genderaffirming care, abortion care, as well as a spectrum of primary and behavioral health care services.
As a mission driven health care provider, we fundamentally believe everyone should be able to access sexual and reproductive health care in their communities, no matter where they live or how much money they make, and we advocate for policies that help make this vision a reality. All people deserve to access comprehensive reproductive health care, including abortion and gender-affirming care, free from shame, stigma, and intimidation. We see everyone who comes to us regardless of ability to pay, and in a typical year, we provide more than $1.25 million dollars in free and discounted care to our communities in Maine. For many, we are their only access to the health care system.
At PPNNE, we have a deep appreciation for the ways that policy and policy implementation, however well-intentioned, impacts the lives of our patients as well as the care we deliver. We have witnessed firsthand policies that disproportionally impact communities of color, leading to starkly different health outcomes. Whether it is how state agencies respond to a public health crisis like a pandemic, policies to address maternal and infant health, or efforts to reduce rates of cancer, outcomes for people of color tell the story of what happens when laws are enacted without careful consideration of potential impact. Racial disparities result from a complex set of factors including socioeconomic disadvantages, resource allocation, and biased decision-making.
1

Robust data collection and analysis are cornerstones for developing and implementing policies that benefit all people in the state. In the 130th session, we supported two bills passed by the legislature and signed by the governor, LD 2 and LD 1610, that strengthened equitable policy development and public access to and engagement with the legislative process. LD 2 and LD 1610 provided legislators with powerful tools to better understand the racial impacts of their proposals and take intentional steps towards developing more equitable policies. These bills also strengthened the state's capacity to collect, analyze, and publish data for policymaking. In the 131st Session we supported an additional bill that was signed into law, LD 1948, further advancing these goals by augmenting the state's capacity for data analysis and enhancing data sharing across state government. LD 590 represents the next step in ensuring our state's policies benefit all Mainers. This legislation will enhance the ability of lawmakers to understand the comprehensive impact of legislation under consideration by authorizing nonpartisan legislative staff to collect racial and other demographic data from state agencies. The more informed this Legislature is with regards to the policies it considers, the more equipped it is to act wisely and prudently in shaping the future of our state. I urge you to vote ought to pass on LD 590.

Testimony of Senator Rachel Talbot Ross
LD 590, "An Act Regarding the Inclusion of Racial and Other Demographic Data from
State Agencies in the Legislative Process."
Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing
Committee on State and Local Government. I am Senator Rachel Talbot Ross. I represent Senate
District 28, which includes part of Portland, part of the Casco Bay Islands, and includes the
University of Southern Maine Campus. I am here today to present LD 590, "An Act Regarding
the Inclusion of Racial and Other Demographic Data from State Agencies in the Legislative
Process."
Back in 2021, during the First Regular Session of the 130th Legislature, Maine took the historic
step in addressing long-standing racial disparities that existed across all systems by enacting LD
2 which did several things:
The first section defines a racial impact statement as an assessment of the potential impact that legislation could have on historically disadvantaged racial populations. ,
The second portion created a study by the Legislative Council to determine the best method in which to establish and implement a system of using racial impact statements.
The third then directed the Legislative Council to conduct a limited pilot project - based on the findings - for the use of racial impact statements in the Second Regular Session of the 130th Legislature. I have a copy of the final report on the pilot for the committee to review at your
convenience.
So, LD 2 defined a racial impact statement, required its usage in the legislative process, and set
out a process to determine the best methodology for implementation.
Very quickly, that process is upon request of a legislative committee, the commissioner of a department or director of an agency is directed to provide data, analysis, and other information necessary for lawmakers to determine whether pending legislation is likely to create or
exacerbate existing racial disparities.

As this committee knows, Maine is not alone in the use of this important data-driven tool in the legislative process. At least nine other states have also implemented mechanisms for the
preparation and consideration of racial impact statements: Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Iowa,
Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, Oregon, and Virginia as well as the District of Columbia and several municipalities across the country including Seattle and New York City.
However, the full implementation of LD 2 - Maine Public Law Chapter 21 - has not been
realized and our goal to proactively prevent new laws from worsening existing racial disparities
and to help undo effects of structural racism has not been met.
I believe that LD 590 is one way to take a step forward in our efforts. This bill requires
nonpartisan legislative staff to collect and assemble racial data from state agencies that is related to legislation before joint standing or select committees of the Legislature.
It also takes another historic step through the inclusion of other demographic data, such as gender, age, socio-economic status, geography, and disability.
With the passage of LD 590, I believe it will encourage lawmakers to pursue more intentional
andequitable policy solutions, rather than relying on race neutral - or gender, age, geographical, socio-economic class, mental or physical ability neutral - approaches that can still produce
disparate results.
With the passage of LD 590, I believe that Maine will truly make the best possible decisions for
our state - now - and for generations to follow.
For these reasons, I urge the committee to support LD 590. Thank you for your time and
consideration.

Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury and members of the Joint Standing
Committee on State and Local Government, my name is Sam Zuckerman. l am the Policy
Coordinator of the Permanent Commission on the Status ot Racial, Indigenous, and Tribal
Populations. l am here today to testify in support of LD 590, "An Act Regarding the Inclusion of
Racial and Other Demographic Data from State Agencies in the Legislative Process."
The Permanent Commission's role is to examine racial disparities across all systems and advise the Maine State Government on ways to improve the status and outcomes of historically disadvantaged racial, Indigenous, and tribal populations. Data is essential to the work that we do because it helps us track disparities over time and to determine which policies are working. Data also helps us to understand why disparities exist and what other issues they intersect with. Data is essential to our ability to address the systemic nature of many of these inequalities.
The Permanent Commission supports LD 590 because it advances Maine's ability to take an evidence-based approach to policymaking by ensuring that demographic data is brought before committees of the Legislature. The Permanent Commission views accurate, consistent, and complete data as critical to understanding the needs and experiences of the diverse population that the Maine State Government serves.
Often, policies that appear to be "race neutral" at face value have disparate impacts on people of color. And these disparate impacts are not limited to any one policy area - health,
education, wealth, and incarceration are all examples of policy areas where laws may be

broadly framed, but where disproportionate outcomes have been documented.` In light of the known disparities, ensuring that demographic data is considered consistently in the legislative process is important for ensuring that systemic disparities are not perpetuated due to a lack of
information.
We urge you to pass this bill to ensure that future legislators have access to all relevant
data when making policy decisions. Thank you for your time. l would be happy to answer any
questions.

Testimony of Sarah Woodbury, Legislative Director, Maine Conservation Voters In Support of LD 590 "An Act Regarding the Inclusion of Racial and Other Demographic
Data from State Agencies in the Legislative Process" Before the Committee on State and Local Government
January 21, 2026
Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury and distinguished members of the Committee on State and Local Government. My name is Sarah Woodbury and I'm the Legislative Director at Maine Conservation Voters. MCV is a statewide non-profit organization with 13,000 members and supporters building a just, thriving future for all by acting on the climate crisis, protecting the environment, and safeguarding our democracy. Please accept this testimony in support of LD 590 "An Act Regarding the Inclusion of Racial and Other Demographic Data from State Agencies in the Legislative Process".
LD 590 is a crucial step in helping the state to utilize the data and analysis capabilities to support equitable policies, public access and engagement that were laid out under LD 1610, passed in the 130th legislative session, and interdepartmental data sharing laid out under LD 1948 which was passed in the 131st legislative session. LD 590 is the next step by creating the position and funding for the role to oversee this data collection and assessment. This bill provides funding for a legislative analyst position in the Office of Policy and Legal Analysis for a period of 4 years to support the work of the office including halftime during session collecting and assembling demographic data from state agencies related to legislation.
It is important for lawmakers to have this information when they are making decisions on legislation that impacts Mainers lives. This data and analysis will help lawmakers to develop anti-racist policies. While racial impact statements will not end structural racism, much like environmental impact statements, they will help legislators make informed decisions before moving forward with policies that will impact those communities. For instance, when looking at impacts of climate change, this data could be used to highlight how low-income communities and communities of color are disproportionately impacted by climate change. It can be used to help legislators come up with specific solutions to mitigate impacts by utilizing the data to come up with specific solutions, such as pollution reduction or green

infrastructure, rather than generic solutions. For these and many other reasons we urge the committee to vote "ought to pass" on LD 590.
Thank you.
